description: Agent-facing evals. This skill ships no script, so there is nothing but prose to test — this file is the whole suite. The characteristic failure of a skill carrying 16 Hard Rejections and a 16-bullet Always Apply list is OVER-REJECTION: an agent primed to hunt web smells starts condemning legitimate native design. So most cases here are deliberately clean, and each clean fixture is built to superficially trip a specific rejection — an iPad grid that reads as a 'dashboard grid', a hero that sits in onboarding rather than 'inside app workflows', a fixed frame that constrains artwork rather than text, a custom bar that has paid the documented-tradeoff toll the Hard Rejections preamble explicitly allows. **A verdict of 'violation' on a clean-* fixture is a FAILURE, not a near-miss.** The dirty variants exist only to prove the agent still discriminates rather than learning 'always say clean'. Run every case WITHOUT the skill first and record the result: a case answered correctly cold is not measuring this skill's guidance and should be cut or hardened, and a case failed identically with the skill loaded means the prose is wrong, not the reader. Fixtures are excerpt-shaped and reference types they do not define — they are read, never built; do not try to compile them.

evals.name: ipad-grid-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/ipad-photo-grid.swift. This is the Library screen of an iPad app running at regular width. Does it contain any native-UX violations? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO. A LazyVGrid of media thumbnails is the native shape for browsable image collections on iPad — Photos, Files icon view, and Music albums all use it. Must NOT fire the 'dashboard grids' Hard Rejection: that rejection is scoped to iPhone ('dashboard grids on iPhone'), and this fixture is explicitly iPad regular width. Adaptive columns, NavigationLink(value:) with a matching navigationDestination, and 16pt spacing are all correct. Flagging this as a web/dashboard smell is the failure this eval exists to catch.

evals.name: glass-toolbar-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/glass-toolbar.swift for Liquid Glass and accessibility problems. Answer with a verdict and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO violations. Glass is applied to a floating control bar — a control/navigation surface, which is exactly where Always Apply says Liquid Glass belongs. Must NOT fire 'icon-only buttons without accessibility labels': the controls use Label("Follow my location", …) with .labelStyle(.iconOnly), so the label text still supplies the accessibility name while only the icon renders. An agent that flags .labelStyle(.iconOnly) as an accessibility violation has pattern-matched on the modifier name without reasoning about what Label provides, and that is a failure. Hit targets are explicit (.frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44) on each label) and the tracking control is a Toggle with .toggleStyle(.button), so selected state reaches VoiceOver via .isSelected rather than through a label that silently changes meaning — both were real defects in the pre-2026-08-04 fixture and neither should now be reported.

evals.name: onboarding-hero-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/onboarding-hero.swift. Our reviewer says it contains a 'hero section', which we reject. Do you agree it should be restructured? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO — do not restructure. The Hard Rejection reads 'hero sections inside app workflows'; first-run onboarding is not an app workflow, and a large lead visual is the platform norm there (Apple's own onboarding and what's-new sheets). Must engage the scope words 'inside app workflows' rather than matching the bare phrase 'hero section'. Credit for noting the screen is otherwise correct: semantic .largeTitle/.body fonts, the decorative SF Symbol carries .accessibilityHidden(true), its size is @ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .largeTitle) so it tracks Dynamic Type, and the content scrolls with the CTA pinned via .safeAreaInset so it cannot be stranded off-screen at AX3–AX5. Answering YES on keyword match is the failure.

evals.name: iphone-tab-root-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/iphone-tab-root.swift, the root view of an iPhone app. Should this navigation structure change? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO. Three flat co-equal top-level sections is exactly the topology TabView owns per Always Apply ('Use TabView for flat top-level app sections'), each wrapping its own NavigationStack for drill-down. The NavigationSplitView guidance is conditioned on collection/detail layouts 'when width supports it' — an iPhone root is neither. Proposing NavigationSplitView here, or treating TabView as suspect because eval 9 rejects it on iPad, is the failure.

evals.name: documented-custom-bar-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/documented-custom-bar.swift. It replaces TabView with a hand-built bar. Should it be rewritten to use TabView? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO. The Hard Rejections preamble states the list applies 'unless the user explicitly asks for them and the tradeoff is documented' — this fixture pays that toll in full: a dated approval, a load-bearing reason TabView cannot serve (SwiftUI exposes no control over system tab-bar height and no way to drive it from an in-progress DragGesture — a constraint no styling or accessory placement removes), an explicit record that TabView was prototyped and rejected on it, and delivered accessibility parity — a visible selected state via .symbolVariant that does not rely on color alone, .isSelected traits, 44pt minimum targets, and the score exposed as .accessibilityLabel plus .accessibilityValue so VoiceOver announces the number rather than replacing it. This eval tests whether the skill's own escape hatch is reachable in practice. Answering YES — rewriting to TabView despite the documented tradeoff — means the rejection list is being applied as absolute and the escape hatch is dead prose.

evals.name: fixed-frame-artwork-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/poster-carousel.swift for Dynamic Type problems. Answer with a verdict and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO Dynamic Type violation. The Hard Rejection is 'fixed-height rows that break Dynamic Type'; here the fixed dimensions constrain the AsyncImage artwork box. The caption shares the column width — as text in any grid column does — but carries no lineLimit and no height cap, and uses .fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true), so it wraps and grows vertically with the user's type size instead of truncating. Must distinguish a fixed frame on an image, and a fixed column width, from a fixed frame that clips text. Flagging the artwork frame is the failure this eval catches. Note the pre-2026-08-04 fixture did truncate (lineLimit(2) inside a width-constrained column) and the cold baseline correctly caught it — that defect is fixed, so re-reporting truncation now is wrong.

evals.name: glass-stat-cards-dirty
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/glass-stat-cards.swift, an iPhone screen. List every native-UX violation you find, most severe first, with a concrete fix for each. Save the review to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md flags violations, at minimum: (1) Liquid Glass used as decorative content-card treatment rather than on controls/navigation — Always Apply rejects exactly this; (2) glass-on-glass — .glassEffect() cards stacked on a .ultraThinMaterial background; (3) thin/light text over translucent material (.fontWeight(.thin), weight: .light) — a legibility and Reduce Transparency failure; (4) decorative gradient carrying hierarchy; (5) hard-coded tiny body text (.system(size: 11)) breaking Dynamic Type; (6) arbitrary Tailwind-style spacing (.padding(15), .padding(11)); (7) dashboard grid on iPhone. Missing the glass-on-glass stacking or the thin-text-over-material pair is a partial failure — those are the two the skill calls out by name and the two a general SwiftUI reviewer is least likely to catch.

evals.name: web-port-dirty
evals.prompt: fixtures/web-port-projects.swift was ported from a React dashboard to SwiftUI for iPhone. Critique it and give a restructuring plan. Save the review to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md identifies this as a web port and prescribes native containers, at minimum: hamburger menu on iPhone → TabView or NavigationStack (the skill rejects hamburger menus on iPhone outright); hand-built 56pt top bar → NavigationStack with a real navigation title and toolbar; marketing hero inside an app workflow → delete, lead with content; two-column card grid on iPhone → List with Sections; right-rail AI panel → not an iPhone shape (sheet, inspector on iPad, or a toolbar entry point); arbitrary .padding(15)/spacing 12 → system spacing; .system(size: 11/13/17/34) → semantic fonts; icon-only bell and hamburger with no accessibility labels. A critique that only restyles — adjusting padding and colors while keeping the hero, grid, and rail — is a failure; the restructuring plan must change containers.

evals.name: concat-a11y-label-dirty
evals.prompt: Audit fixtures/tier-row-a11y.swift for VoiceOver problems and give the corrected accessibility modifiers. Save the audit to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md flags the single concatenated .accessibilityLabel that swallows the rank (a value), the subtitle, and the reorder instruction (a hint) into one string, and splits them by semantic role: .accessibilityLabel(item.title), .accessibilityValue("Rank \(rank)"), .accessibilityHint for the reorder affordance. Must also catch that .accessibilityElement(children: .ignore) makes the reorder Button unreachable to VoiceOver — the label's own instruction to 'double tap the reorder button' is therefore impossible to follow, which is the sharper bug. Fix is .accessibilityElement(children: .combine) with the button kept as its own element, or an explicit .accessibilityAction. Catching the concatenation but not the unreachable button is a partial pass.

evals.name: ipad-tab-root-dirty
evals.prompt: fixtures/ipad-tab-root.swift is the root view of an iPad app at regular width. Does the navigation structure need to change? Answer YES (needs changing) or NO (ship as is), justify, and give the corrected structure. Save to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers YES and proposes NavigationSplitView for the Library tab — but locates the defect in the TOPOLOGY, not the container. TabView is a legitimate iPad root; with .tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable) it is Apple's own iPad direction from iPadOS 18 onward (WWDC24 'Elevate your tab and sidebar experience in iPadOS'). What is wrong is wrapping a collection/detail hierarchy in a full-width NavigationStack, so selecting a collection slides the entire canvas away. Corrected structure: NavigationSplitView with the collection list as sidebar and CollectionDetail as detail. Credit for spotting the missing .tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable) and Tab(role: .search). A verdict that rejects TabView-as-iPad-root per se is WRONG — it contradicts Apple and references/ipad-layout.md, and it is the exact error this eval exists to catch, because SKILL.md asserted it until the 2026-08-02 baseline run disproved it. Must NOT contradict eval 3: the distinction is topology, not iPhone-vs-iPad.
